solution.brief: Wasp 0.6 basic aggregation tutorial: defines a hexagonal part with 6 connection faces, creates bidirectional rules, and runs stochastic aggregation to grow a discrete assembly.
solution.principle:
Related insight: Related insight: This single-hex-part foundation extends to multi-part assemblies where two or more distinct Brep-based parts are defined, each with their own connections. In multi-part setups, assembly rules are typically expressed as text strings encoding part-name and connection-index pairs, enabling rule-driven growth across a vocabulary of part types. The stochastic aggregation engine handles multi-part rule sets without architectural changes.

Related insight: Related insight: Beyond Brep-based parts with face connections, Wasp supports mesh geometry where connection planes are derived from mesh vertices and edges. This mesh-topology approach (tutorial 03) provides an alternative part-definition pathway that avoids explicit direction-curve authoring — connections emerge from the mesh structure itself.

Related insight: Related insight: The Wasp aggregation visualization pipeline can be extended with Weaverbird Catmull-Clark subdivision. After extracting part geometry from the aggregation, Weaverbird can smooth the resulting mesh — providing a continuous, subdivided preview of the discrete assembly. This post-processing step is introduced in tutorial 04 and is compatible with both single-part and multi-part aggregation setups.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 06 demonstrates that WaspPart definitions can carry custom attributes (metadata per part type) and that aggregation results can be exported to disk via a file update component. These capabilities extend the foundational aggregation workflow beyond visualization into data annotation and persistence.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 01 (wasp_01_basic_aggregation) is the minimal entry-point for the Wasp workflow — it introduces the same 5-step pattern (geometry → connections → WaspPart → Rules → Stochastic Aggregation) with a simpler part before this hexagonal 6-connection example. Learners encountering Wasp for the first time should start with tutorial 01 before this more detailed hex-part tutorial.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 02 (wasp_02_rule_grammar) specifically addresses rule grammar — how multiple rules encode directionality to govern which connections can mate and in what orientation. The bidirectional rule pairs introduced in this hex-part tutorial are the simplest case of a rule grammar; tutorial 02 generalizes this to multi-rule systems where connection compatibility is explicitly specified as a grammar over the part vocabulary.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial wasp_04_field_driven demonstrates that Wasp stochastic aggregation can be biased by scalar fields — attractor-based or density-gradient fields influence which parts are placed and where, steering growth beyond purely random selection. This field-driven approach is an advanced extension of the foundational stochastic aggregation workflow introduced here, adding directed spatial intent to the otherwise uniform random growth.

Related insight: Related insight: Tutorial 05 (wasp_05_collider) extends the foundational stochastic aggregation workflow with collider and containment — collision detection between aggregated parts and boundary BRep geometry constrains growth within a defined volume. This intermediate feature builds directly on the basic aggregation workflow established here, adding spatial boundary enforcement as a growth-control mechanism.

intents: build modular assembly with random growth

evolution_history.changes: New pattern is a direct multi-part extension of this single-part tutorial. Adding multi-part and text-rules context helps users understand the progression from this foundation.

New pattern introduces mesh-based connection derivation as an alternative to the Brep/face approach, which is useful context for understanding the range of part-definition strategies available in Wasp.

The base aggregation foundation pattern should document that Weaverbird subdivision is an available visualization enhancement, so users progressing through tutorials understand the full range of output options.
The hex-part foundation pattern should note the custom attributes and file export capabilities introduced in tutorial 06.

The new pattern explicitly identifies itself as the beginner/prerequisite tutorial 01. The hex-part tutorial (5c0baa38) is a natural next step and should reference tutorial 01 as its prerequisite entry point. Adding beginner/prerequisite tags and lineage context improves discoverability and learning path clarity.

This hex-part aggregation pattern introduces bidirectional rules as a foundation; the new rule grammar pattern extends that concept to multi-rule grammars, so the neighbor gains forward-pointing context and relevant tags.
The foundational aggregation pattern should reference the field-driven extension as an advanced pathway learners can progress toward.

This hex-part foundation tutorial should reference the collider/containment extension introduced in tutorial 05, helping learners understand how the basic workflow evolves toward spatially bounded assembly.
